overview: Kamarupa was a kingdom centred on the Brahmaputra valley, with major regional influence under Bhaskaravarman in the seventh century. The map’s approximate 600-700 window highlights this phase, not the kingdom’s entire lifetime. Its broad outline extends beyond the core valley and cannot establish the king’s control over every enclosed place.

periods.title: Earlier foundations
periods.summary: Bhutivarman’s earlier grant became the basis of a later renewal.

periods.title: Bhaskaravarman’s generation
periods.summary: Diplomacy linked Kamarupa with Harsha’s northern Indian court.

periods.title: An uncertain transition
periods.summary: Bhaskaravarman died around 650; the subsequent transfer of power remains unclear.

sections.title: A regional power and its royal stories

items.text: Bana’s Harshacharita describes Bhaskaravarman’s envoy Hamsavega seeking an alliance with Harsha against their common rival, Shashanka of Gauda. This poetic court biography places Kamarupa within the struggle for power across northern and eastern India, rather than at its isolated edge.

The embassy’s gifts included an elaborate parasol associated with royalty. In this account, an umbrella could announce political rank as well as keep someone shaded. The wonderful stories told about its ancient owners belong to the author’s literary presentation.

Bana also describes pearls, jewels and silk towels packed in baskets among the gifts. The list gives a vivid picture of the luxurious objects a court could display in diplomacy. It does not tell us that every household owned such expensive things.

Royal inscriptions connected the Varman rulers with Naraka and Bhagadatta, figures of religious and epic tradition. These genealogies helped justify kingship. Their enormous spans of legendary time cannot be read as a dated list of historically documented rulers.

The Nidhanpur charter was issued from a camp at Karnasuvarna. Its introduction celebrates ships, elephants, horses and foot soldiers. These are the military resources the court wished to advertise; the praise supplies no reliable headcount for the army.

sections.title: Land, families and the changing river

items.text: The Nidhanpur grant renewed an older award of land to Brahmans. When the previous copper charter was lost, the land had become liable for revenue. Replacing the document restored the exemption: keeping the paperwork safe could have very practical consequences for a family.

Rivers could redraw the fields. The charter specifies who should receive the produce or land added by the Kausika and Gangini rivers. Officials needed rules for a landscape that changed with water and sediment, even when a boundary had once seemed settled.

Seven shares were reserved for worship, offerings and hospitality. The grant supported religious and social obligations as well as individual recipients. Here the translated word hospitality should not be mistaken for evidence of a medical hospital.

The grantee list names Srivasu with three brothers and records affiliations with particular Vedic traditions. It preserves family relationships and specialist religious learning among the recipients. It is not a register of every family or a survey of village schools.

sections.title: The people who made the grant work

items.text: A potter’s pit appears among the landmarks defining the granted land. Behind the king’s grand language is a place where someone dug or worked clay. Everyday craft sites could be familiar enough to help neighbours identify a legal boundary.

The record names a metalworker, Kaliya, in connection with producing the charter. A copper document required practical skill as well as fine Sanskrit. This is a rare chance to encounter a working person’s name alongside those of rulers and religious recipients.

The charter’s business involved a local headman, a legal official and a clerk, among others. Marking boundaries and recording rights required cooperation between the court and people who knew the locality. Royal instructions still needed someone to carry them out on the ground.

At Dah-Parbatia near Tezpur, a carved stone temple doorway is dated stylistically to about the sixth century. It predates this map window and shows the architectural world inherited by seventh-century Kamarupa. Its date does not identify Bhaskaravarman as the builder.

The doorway’s carvings include the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna, garlands and carefully arranged floral bands. Stoneworkers turned an entrance into a richly decorated religious setting. Close looking reveals the smaller carved details that a distant view of the monument can hide.

The Nidhanpur plates came to light in December 1912 when a farmer levelled a mound for a buffalo shed. Their seal and copper surfaces attracted attention; scholars eventually recognized a royal grant. An ordinary building job had uncovered a much older legal record.

The charter explains that an earlier document had burned and that the replacement used different-looking letters. It insists that the changed handwriting did not make the grant false. Historians must therefore study the surviving copy and its own account of how it came to exist.

Sanskrit: “प्रणम्य देवं” (praṇamya devaṃ), “Having saluted the god.” This opens the surviving Nidhanpur charter’s invocation to Shiva. The phrase is shown in modern Devanagari and normalized transliteration, rather than the document’s old letterforms; it represents formal religious writing, not everyone’s everyday speech.

ending.text: Bhaskaravarman died around 650, probably without children. The precise succession is uncertain; later records associate Salastambha with the transfer of power. Kamarupa continued under later ruling houses. The map’s 700 endpoint marks neither the disappearance of its people nor the end of the kingdom’s wider history.
